cards.title: friend
cards.meaning: A person you know and like.
cards.example: Mia is my friend.
cards.conversation:
A: Is Ben your friend?
B: Yes, he is.
cards.exercise: Complete: Mia is my ____.
cards.answer: friend
cards.synonymNote: Pal is informal; these words can differ in closeness.
cards.notes: Say my friend, your friend, or our friend. Use friends for two or more people.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating friend.

cards.title: share
cards.meaning: To use or enjoy something with another person.
cards.example: We share an apple.
cards.conversation:
A: Can we share this cake?
B: Yes, of course.
cards.exercise: Complete: We ____ an apple.
cards.answer: share
cards.synonymNote: These explain the meaning; they do not fit every sentence in the same way.
cards.notes: Say share something with someone: I share my cake with Mia.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating share.

cards.title: come in
cards.meaning: To enter a room or a home.
cards.example: Please come in.
cards.conversation:
A: Hello, Mia!
B: Hi! Please come in.
cards.exercise: Invite a friend inside using two words.
cards.answer: Come in.
cards.notes: Say Please come in when a person is at your door.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating come in.

cards.title: sit down
cards.meaning: To move into a sitting position.
cards.example: Please sit down here.
cards.conversation:
A: Can I sit here?
B: Yes. Please sit down.
cards.exercise: Complete: Please sit ____ here.
cards.answer: down
cards.notes: Please makes the request friendly: Please sit down.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating sit down.

cards.title: a big help
cards.meaning: A person or thing that helps you a lot.
cards.example: You are a big help.
cards.conversation:
A: Here are the cups.
B: Thank you. You are a big help.
cards.exercise: Thank a helpful friend: You are a ____ help.
cards.answer: big
cards.notes: Say You are a big help to thank someone.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating a big help.

cards.title: no problem
cards.meaning: A friendly reply meaning that you are happy to help.
cards.example: “Thank you!” “No problem!”
cards.conversation:
A: Can you help me?
B: No problem.
cards.exercise: Reply to “Thank you!” with this expression.
cards.answer: No problem.
cards.notes: Use it after a request or after Thank you.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating no problem.

cards.title: Let’s make lunch together.
cards.meaning: A friendly way to ask someone to make lunch with you.
cards.example: Let’s make lunch together.
cards.conversation:
A: I am hungry.
B: Let’s make lunch together.
cards.exercise: Complete: Let’s ____ lunch together.
cards.answer: make
synonyms: Shall we prepare lunch as a team?
Would you like to help me cook lunch?
cards.notes: Use Let's + a verb: Let's cook. Let's eat. Let's share.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Let’s make lunch together..

cards.title: A small act can make a good day.
cards.meaning: One kind thing can help someone have a happy day.
cards.example: I help my friend. A small act can make a good day.
cards.conversation:
A: Here is some water for you.
B: Thank you. That is kind.
cards.exercise: Write one small act of kindness in English.
cards.answer: I share my lunch.
synonyms: One kind gesture can brighten a day.
Little acts of care can lift someone’s spirits.
cards.notes: Read this as a reflection, not a factual rule. Relate it to a specific action in the example, and explain why you agree or disagree.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating A small act can make a good day..

cards.title: We + verb
cards.meaning: Use we with the base form of a verb to say what you do together.
cards.example: We cook lunch. We share the food.
cards.conversation:
A: What do you do together?
B: We cook and talk.
cards.exercise: Choose: We (share / shares) the food.
cards.answer: We share the food.
cards.notes: Say We cook, not We cooks. Say We share, not We shares.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating We + verb.

cards.title: Would you like some tea?
cards.meaning: A polite way to offer someone tea.
cards.example: Would you like some tea?
cards.conversation:
A: Would you like some tea?
B: Yes, please. Thank you.
cards.exercise: Answer politely if you do not want tea.
cards.answer: No, thank you.
cards.notes: Answer Yes, please or No, thank you.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Would you like some tea?.

cards.title: Lunch with a friend
cards.meaning: A short story about two friends making and sharing lunch.
paragraphs: Lunch with my friend Mia is fun. We make food and help each other.
First, we make lunch together. I wash an apple. Mia makes two sandwiches. We sit down and share the food.
We also help each other. After lunch, Mia washes the cups. I put them away. She is a big help.
Lunch with Mia is a good time. We have nice food and work together. I am happy with my friend.
cards.exercise: Who makes the sandwiches? Write one sentence.
cards.answer: Mia makes the sandwiches.
cards.example: We use “Lunch with a friend” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Main idea: lunch is fun. Reason 1: making food. Reason 2: helping. End: say why the time is good.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Lunch with a friend.

cards.title: prepare
cards.meaning: To make something ready before you use it or need it.
cards.example: We need to prepare lunch before we leave.
cards.conversation:
A: Is everything ready?
B: Almost. I need to prepare the fruit.
cards.exercise: Complete: We need to ____ lunch.
cards.answer: prepare
cards.synonymNote: Use get ready for yourself; make ready usually takes a thing.
cards.notes: You can prepare food, a bag, or a room. Prepare for + an event: prepare for a picnic.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating prepare.

cards.title: plan
cards.meaning: An idea or arrangement for what you will do.
cards.example: Our plan is to meet at ten.
cards.conversation:
A: What is the plan for Sunday?
B: We are having a picnic.
cards.exercise: Complete: Our ____ is to meet at ten.
cards.answer: plan
cards.synonymNote: Idea is more general; an arrangement is usually more definite.
cards.notes: Use a plan for + a noun: a plan for Sunday. Use plan to + a verb when plan is a verb.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating plan.

cards.title: bring along
cards.meaning: To take someone or something with you.
cards.example: Please bring along a bottle of water.
cards.conversation:
A: What should I bring along?
B: Some water and a hat.
cards.exercise: Complete: Please bring ____ a hat.
cards.answer: along
cards.notes: Say bring along a hat or bring a hat along. With it, say bring it along.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating bring along.
cards.displayTitle:
bring something along
bring along something

cards.title: take turns
cards.meaning: To do something one after another.
cards.example: We take turns carrying the picnic bag.
cards.conversation:
A: This bag is heavy.
B: Let’s take turns carrying it.
cards.exercise: Complete: We take ____ carrying the bag.
cards.answer: turns
cards.notes: Use take turns + -ing: We take turns carrying the bag.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating take turns.

cards.title: lend a hand
cards.meaning: To help someone with a task.
cards.example: Can you lend a hand with the bags?
cards.conversation:
A: Can you lend a hand?
B: Sure. I can carry this bag.
cards.exercise: Ask a friend to help using “lend”.
cards.answer: Can you lend a hand?
cards.notes: Say lend a hand with the bags. This means help; it is not about giving someone your hand.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating lend a hand.

cards.title: on the same page
cards.meaning: To understand or agree about the same thing.
cards.example: We are on the same page about the meeting time.
cards.conversation:
A: We meet at ten, right?
B: Yes. We are on the same page.
cards.exercise: What does “on the same page” mean here?
cards.answer: We understand the plan in the same way.
cards.notes: This is an informal expression. Check a simple detail first: We meet at ten, right?
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating on the same page.

cards.title: I can bring fruit if you bring bread.
cards.meaning: A way to suggest that each person brings part of the food.
cards.example: I can bring fruit if you bring bread.
cards.conversation:
A: What should we each bring?
B: I can bring fruit if you bring bread.
cards.exercise: Complete: I can bring fruit ____ you bring bread.
cards.answer: if
synonyms: Shall I bring fruit while you bring bread?
We could each bring part of the food.
cards.notes: Use if to connect the two parts of the plan. Here it means one plan depends on the other.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating I can bring fruit if you bring bread..

cards.title: A shared plan leaves more time to enjoy the day.
cards.meaning: Planning together can give people more time to enjoy an activity.
cards.example: We decide who will bring lunch. A shared plan leaves more time to enjoy the day.
cards.conversation:
A: Everything is ready now.
B: Great. We can enjoy the picnic.
cards.exercise: Name one task you can do before a picnic.
cards.answer: I can prepare the sandwiches.
synonyms: Planning together creates room for enjoyment.
A little coordination frees up time.
cards.notes: Read this as a reflection, not a factual rule. Relate it to a specific action in the example, and explain why you agree or disagree.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating A shared plan leaves more time to enjoy the day..

cards.title: Be going to + verb
cards.meaning: Use am, is, or are going to + a verb for a plan you have already made.
cards.example: We are going to meet near the lake.
cards.conversation:
A: What are you going to bring?
B: I am going to bring fruit.
cards.exercise: Complete: She ____ going to bring a blanket.
cards.answer: is
cards.notes: Match be to the person: I am, she is, we are going to meet.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Be going to + verb.

cards.title: Do you have any plans for Sunday?
cards.meaning: A friendly question about someone's Sunday plans.
cards.example: Do you have any plans for Sunday?
cards.conversation:
A: Do you have any plans for Sunday?
B: Yes, I am going to a picnic. Would you like to come?
cards.exercise: Invite your friend to the picnic.
cards.answer: Would you like to come to our picnic?
cards.notes: After the answer, ask about the activity or invite the person to join you.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Do you have any plans for Sunday?.

cards.title: A picnic that works for everyone
cards.meaning: A story about friends planning a picnic and helping one another.
paragraphs: A picnic is more fun when friends plan ahead and help each other. Our picnic near the lake on Sunday is a good example.
First, a clear plan helps us prepare. We are going to meet at ten. I am going to bring sandwiches, Lina can bring fruit, and Omar can bring water. Everyone knows what to do.
Second, helping each other makes the work easier. Omar has a heavy bag, so we take turns carrying it. After lunch, we all help to clean up.
Planning and helping make our picnic a good day for everyone. We enjoy our food and our time together. Next time, we want to work together again.
cards.exercise: How do the friends help Omar?
cards.answer: They take turns carrying his heavy bag.
cards.example: We use “A picnic that works for everyone” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Introduce two reasons. Explain planning with an example. Explain helping with an example. Restate both reasons.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating A picnic that works for everyone.

A2.source: demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: contribute
cards.meaning: To give time, money, skills, or ideas to help a shared goal.
cards.example: Everyone can contribute an idea to the garden project.
cards.conversation:
A: I do not know much about plants.
B: You can still contribute your drawing skills.
cards.exercise: Complete: Everyone can ____ an idea.
cards.answer: contribute
cards.synonymNote: The shared purpose is important when using contribute.
cards.notes: Use contribute something to a project. You can also contribute by helping with a task.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating contribute.

cards.title: responsibility
cards.meaning: A task or duty that you are expected to take care of.
cards.example: Watering the plants is my responsibility this week.
cards.conversation:
A: Who will check the plants?
B: That is my responsibility.
cards.exercise: Name one responsibility in a shared garden.
cards.answer: Watering the plants is one responsibility.
cards.synonymNote: Duty and obligation may suggest stronger requirements.
cards.notes: Use responsibility for + a noun or -ing: responsibility for watering the plants.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating responsibility.

cards.title: work out
cards.meaning: To find an answer or plan by thinking about it.
cards.example: We need to work out a watering schedule.
cards.conversation:
A: We cannot come every day.
B: Let’s work out a schedule together.
cards.exercise: Complete: We need to work ____ a schedule.
cards.answer: out
cards.notes: In this lesson, work out means solve or plan, not exercise. Say work it out with a pronoun.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating work out.
cards.displayTitle:
work something out
work out something

cards.title: follow through
cards.meaning: To complete something you have promised or started.
cards.example: It matters that we follow through on our promises.
cards.conversation:
A: You said you would buy seeds.
B: Yes. I will follow through this afternoon.
cards.exercise: Complete: We should follow ____ on our promises.
cards.answer: through
cards.notes: Use follow through on a promise or a plan. The expression focuses on taking action.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating follow through.

cards.title: pull your weight
cards.meaning: To do your fair share of the work.
cards.example: The garden succeeds when everyone pulls their weight.
cards.conversation:
A: How can we keep the work fair?
B: Everyone needs to pull their weight.
cards.exercise: Explain “pull your weight” in simple English.
cards.answer: Do your fair share of the work.
cards.notes: This is informal. Telling someone to pull their weight may sound critical, so use it with care.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating pull your weight.

cards.title: many hands make light work
cards.meaning: A saying that work becomes easier when many people help.
cards.example: We finished planting quickly: many hands make light work.
cards.conversation:
A: That was faster than I expected.
B: Many hands make light work.
cards.exercise: Complete: Many hands make ____ work.
cards.answer: light
cards.notes: Use the whole saying after a group finishes a task. It does not refer to the weight of people's hands.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating many hands make light work.

cards.title: Could we agree on who will do each task?
cards.meaning: A polite way to ask a group to decide who is responsible for each job.
cards.example: Could we agree on who will do each task before we start?
cards.conversation:
A: We have seeds and tools.
B: Great. Could we agree on who will do each task?
cards.exercise: Rewrite politely: “Tell me who does each task.”
cards.answer: Could we agree on who will do each task?
synonyms: Can we divide up the jobs?
Shall we decide who is responsible for what?
cards.notes: Could we makes the request cooperative. Follow it with a clear task or decision.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Could we agree on who will do each task?.

cards.title: Trust grows when small promises become actions.
cards.meaning: People learn to trust each other when promises are kept.
cards.example: She arrives every Saturday as promised. Trust grows when small promises become actions.
cards.conversation:
A: Can we depend on Rosa?
B: Yes. She always does what she promises.
cards.exercise: Describe one action that builds trust.
cards.answer: Arriving when you promised builds trust.
cards.notes: Read this as a reflection, not a factual rule. Relate it to a specific action in the example, and explain why you agree or disagree.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Trust grows when small promises become actions..

cards.title: If + present, will + verb
cards.meaning: Use if + present simple and will + a verb for a possible future condition and result.
cards.example: If we share the work, we will finish before lunch.
cards.conversation:
A: Will the garden be ready?
B: If everyone helps, we will finish today.
cards.exercise: Complete: If it rains, we ____ work indoors.
cards.answer: will
cards.notes: The if-part uses the present: If it rains, not If it will rain.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating If + present, will + verb.

cards.title: How did you get interested in gardening?
cards.meaning: An open question about how someone's interest in gardening began.
cards.example: How did you get interested in gardening?
cards.conversation:
A: How did you get interested in gardening?
B: My grandfather taught me. What about you?
cards.exercise: Ask a follow-up question about this hobby.
cards.answer: What do you enjoy growing most?
cards.notes: Get interested in + a noun or -ing. Follow up with a question about what the person enjoys.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating How did you get interested in gardening?.

cards.title: Growing something together
cards.meaning: How a community garden teaches neighbours to share responsibility and follow through.
paragraphs: A community garden needs more than seeds and tools. Our neighbourhood project showed that sharing responsibility and communicating clearly help people work well together.

First, dividing the work gives everyone a way to contribute. We started small: two neighbours brought tools, while others bought seeds. We also worked out a watering schedule so that the garden was never just one person’s responsibility.

Second, clear communication helps a group solve problems. When someone forgot to water the plants, we checked the schedule together. We made the instructions clearer instead of blaming the person, so everyone could follow through.

The garden taught us two useful lessons: share the work fairly and discuss problems openly. These habits helped our plants grow and made us a stronger team. Other community projects can benefit from the same approach.
cards.exercise: Why did the neighbours make the instructions clearer?
cards.answer: Someone had forgotten a task, so clearer instructions could help everyone understand their responsibilities.
cards.example: We use “Growing something together” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Claim: teamwork needs shared duties and clear communication. Develop each reason with a garden example. Reconnect both reasons to the claim.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Growing something together.

B1.source: demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: coordinate
cards.meaning: To organise people or activities so that they work well together.
cards.example: We need to coordinate the exhibition with the library team.
cards.conversation:
A: Who is managing the schedule?
B: Maya will coordinate the different groups.
A: Should we send her our available dates?
B: Yes, that will help her avoid clashes.
cards.exercise: Complete: Maya will ____ the different groups.
cards.answer: coordinate
cards.synonymNote: Coordinate emphasises how different parts work together.
cards.notes: Coordinate a project, a team, or a schedule. Coordinate with someone identifies a partner in the planning.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating coordinate.

cards.title: constraint
cards.meaning: A condition that limits what is possible.
cards.example: Our main constraint is the size of the room.
cards.conversation:
A: Why can’t we add another display?
B: Space is our biggest constraint.
A: Could we use the corridor as well?
B: Possibly, if the library approves it.
cards.exercise: Name a possible constraint on an exhibition.
cards.answer: A limited budget is a possible constraint.
cards.synonymNote: A constraint can be practical, rather than a rule imposed by someone.
cards.notes: Common combinations include time constraints, budget constraints, and practical constraints.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating constraint.

cards.title: map out
cards.meaning: To plan something in detail before doing it.
cards.example: Let’s map out the visitor’s journey before designing signs.
cards.conversation:
A: Where should visitors go first?
B: We need to map out the whole route.
A: Should the welcome panel come first?
B: Yes, then the displays can follow a clear sequence.
cards.exercise: Complete: Let’s map ____ the visitor’s journey.
cards.answer: out
cards.notes: Map out a route, a process, or a strategy. With a pronoun, say map it out.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating map out.
cards.displayTitle:
map something out
map out something

cards.title: check in with
cards.meaning: To contact someone briefly to learn how things are going.
cards.example: I will check in with the designer on Thursday.
cards.conversation:
A: Have the labels been approved?
B: I will check in with the designer today.
A: Could you ask about the final deadline too?
B: Of course. I will confirm both details.
cards.exercise: Write a sentence arranging a progress check.
cards.answer: I will check in with the team tomorrow.
cards.notes: Check in with a person and check on a task. Here, check in does not mean registering at a hotel.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating check in with.

cards.title: get the ball rolling
cards.meaning: To start an activity or process.
cards.example: A short workshop will get the ball rolling.
cards.conversation:
A: How should we begin?
B: Let’s get the ball rolling with a few sketches.
A: Could each group suggest one idea?
B: That would give us something concrete to discuss.
cards.exercise: Explain this expression in plain English.
cards.answer: Start an activity or process.
cards.notes: Often used when a team needs an initial action. A question, sketch, or meeting can get the ball rolling.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating get the ball rolling.

cards.title: iron out the wrinkles
cards.meaning: To solve small problems in a plan or process.
cards.example: The trial run helped us iron out the wrinkles.
cards.conversation:
A: Did the test reveal any problems?
B: A few, but we have time to iron out the wrinkles.
A: Which issue needs attention first?
B: The signs near the entrance are still confusing.
cards.exercise: What sort of problems are “wrinkles” here?
cards.answer: Small practical problems in the plan.
cards.notes: Wrinkles is a metaphor for practical difficulties. The expression suggests refinement rather than a complete redesign.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating iron out the wrinkles.

cards.title: What would make this plan workable for everyone?
cards.meaning: A question inviting people to identify changes that would make a plan practical.
cards.example: What would make this plan workable for everyone involved?
cards.conversation:
A: Some volunteers cannot arrive early.
B: What would make this plan workable for everyone?
A: Could we divide the setup into two shifts?
B: That would let more people take part.
cards.exercise: Replace “possible to carry out” with one word.
cards.answer: workable
synonyms: How could we adapt the plan to suit the group?
What changes would make this practical for all of us?
cards.notes: Workable means possible to carry out. The question invites solutions without assuming everyone has the same needs.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating What would make this plan workable for everyone?.

cards.title: Clarity is a form of care in a shared project.
cards.meaning: Clear communication can show consideration for the people doing shared work.
cards.example: A clear brief saves people from guessing. Clarity is a form of care in a shared project.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did you rewrite the brief?
B: I wanted everyone to know what was expected.
A: Did the volunteers find it useful?
B: Yes. They could plan their time without guessing.
cards.exercise: Give an example of clarity helping a team.
cards.answer: A clear deadline helps teammates plan their work.
synonyms: Good communication helps people work together.
cards.notes: Read this as a reflection, not a factual rule. Relate it to a specific action in the example, and explain why you agree or disagree.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Clarity is a form of care in a shared project..

cards.title: If we had…, we could…
cards.meaning: Use if + past simple and could + a verb to discuss an imagined situation and a possible result.
cards.example: If we had a larger room, we could include more exhibits.
cards.conversation:
A: Could we add a reading corner?
B: If we had more space, we could.
A: What can we do with the room we have?
B: We could use a smaller display and keep the entrance clear.
cards.exercise: Complete: If we ____ more time, we could test another design.
cards.answer: had
cards.notes: The past form often signals distance from reality, not past time: If we had more space, we could expand.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating If we had…, we could….

cards.title: What has been the most rewarding part so far?
cards.meaning: A friendly question about what has felt most worthwhile during a project.
cards.example: What has been the most rewarding part of the project so far?
cards.conversation:
A: What has been the most rewarding part so far?
B: Seeing ideas from different people come together.
A: Was there a moment when that became clear?
B: Yes, during the first trial run with visitors.
cards.exercise: Ask a follow-up about a challenge.
cards.answer: What has been the biggest challenge so far?
cards.notes: So far means from the start until now. Rewarding asks about satisfaction, rather than financial payment.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating What has been the most rewarding part so far?.

cards.title: A good plan makes room for people
cards.meaning: How clear planning and practical flexibility help people collaborate confidently.
paragraphs: A good collaborative plan should provide direction while leaving room for change. Preparing a small exhibition at our neighbourhood library taught us that shared priorities and practical testing make this balance possible.

First, agreeing on constraints gives a team a useful starting point. With a narrow room and a modest budget, we mapped out the visitor’s journey before choosing displays. This shared reference point helped us decide which ideas were workable.

Second, testing a plan makes flexibility practical. Our trial run revealed that the entrance would become crowded. We moved the introductory panel further inside, solving the problem before it required a costly last-minute change.

Effective coordination therefore combines clear priorities with opportunities to adjust. By making decisions visible and checking in before the deadline, a team can remain organised without becoming rigid. That is what makes a plan work for people.
cards.exercise: What did the trial run reveal, and how did the team respond?
cards.answer: It revealed that the entrance would become crowded. The team moved the introductory panel further inside.
cards.example: We use “A good plan makes room for people” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Thesis: direction plus flexibility. Body 1: shared priorities, with a planning example. Body 2: testing, with a revision example. Conclude by connecting both.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating A good plan makes room for people.

B2.source: demonstration edition; original card format, level-specific English content.

cards.title: interdependence
cards.meaning: A situation in which people or things depend on one another.
cards.example: The project’s interdependence made isolated planning ineffective.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did one delay affect three teams?
B: The level of interdependence was higher than we realised.
A: Would separate deadlines help?
B: Only if we also made the dependencies explicit.
cards.exercise: Complete: Their mutual reliance reflects a high degree of ____.
cards.answer: interdependence
cards.synonymNote: These describe reliance in both directions.
cards.notes: Usually uncountable. Interdependence between teams means one team's decisions can affect another's work.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating interdependence.

cards.title: reconcile
cards.meaning: To make apparently conflicting ideas, needs, or demands compatible.
cards.example: We must reconcile creative ambition with the available time.
cards.conversation:
A: Can we preserve the idea and meet the deadline?
B: We need to reconcile those competing demands.
A: Which part of the design is essential?
B: The accessible route matters more than the extra display.
cards.exercise: Complete: We must ____ ambition with available time.
cards.answer: reconcile
cards.synonymNote: These apply to the sense of reconciling competing ideas or demands.
cards.notes: Use reconcile one demand with another. This sense concerns compatibility, not necessarily repairing a personal relationship.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating reconcile.

cards.title: account for
cards.meaning: To take a relevant factor into consideration.
cards.example: The timeline should account for feedback from volunteers.
cards.conversation:
A: Is the schedule realistic?
B: Only if it accounts for the review process.
A: Could we shorten the review?
B: Perhaps, but we should not remove the people it is meant to include.
cards.exercise: Rewrite: “Include accessibility needs in the plan.”
cards.answer: Account for accessibility needs in the plan.
cards.notes: Here account for means allow for something in planning. In another context, it can mean explain a cause.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating account for.

cards.title: build on
cards.meaning: To use an existing achievement, idea, or resource as a basis for further development.
cards.example: The revised proposal builds on what residents told us.
cards.conversation:
A: Are we discarding the first draft?
B: No. We are building on its strongest ideas.
A: Which element is worth keeping?
B: The visitor feedback gives us a strong starting point.
cards.exercise: Complete: The proposal builds ____ earlier feedback.
cards.answer: on
cards.notes: Build on feedback or experience. The expression stresses continuity rather than replacing everything that came before.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating build on.

cards.title: see the wood for the trees
cards.meaning: To recognise the overall situation without becoming distracted by details.
cards.example: We were so focused on wording that we could not see the wood for the trees.
cards.conversation:
A: Are these tiny edits helping?
B: Perhaps we need to step back and see the wood for the trees.
A: What is the exhibition meant to achieve?
B: It should help residents see their experiences represented.
cards.exercise: What is the equivalent American expression?
cards.answer: See the forest for the trees.
cards.notes: Usually found with can't or couldn't. This is the British form; American English commonly uses forest instead of wood.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating see the wood for the trees.

cards.title: meet halfway
cards.meaning: To reach a compromise in which both sides make concessions.
cards.example: Both teams agreed to meet halfway on the format.
cards.conversation:
A: They want a long report, but we prefer a short one.
B: Could we meet halfway with a summary and an appendix?
A: Would both teams accept that?
B: They might, provided the appendix remains easy to find.
cards.exercise: Suggest a compromise using “meet halfway”.
cards.answer: We could meet halfway by keeping the summary short and adding an appendix.
cards.notes: It need not mean a mathematically equal split. The emphasis is on reciprocal willingness to adjust.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating meet halfway.

cards.title: Before we optimise the process, let’s clarify its purpose.
cards.meaning: A reminder to establish what a process is for before trying to make it more efficient.
cards.example: Before we optimise the process, let’s clarify its purpose.
cards.conversation:
A: Could we make the review faster?
B: Yes, but first let’s clarify what it is intended to achieve.
A: What is the review supposed to protect?
B: Accuracy, accessibility, and the chance to challenge assumptions.
cards.exercise: Paraphrase “clarify its purpose”.
cards.answer: Make clear what it is meant to achieve.
synonyms: Let’s establish the goal before improving the method.
First ask what the procedure is meant to achieve.
cards.notes: Optimise concerns how well a process works; clarify its purpose asks whether the intended goal is understood.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Before we optimise the process, let’s clarify its purpose..

cards.title: Good collaboration makes disagreement usable.
cards.meaning: Constructive cooperation can turn differences of opinion into useful insight.
cards.example: Different views helped us identify a weak assumption. Good collaboration makes disagreement usable.
cards.conversation:
A: I thought disagreement would slow us down.
B: It helped us ask a better question.
A: What made the objection useful?
B: It pointed to a need we had not yet considered.
cards.exercise: Explain how disagreement can help a project.
cards.answer: It can expose assumptions that a like-minded group might overlook.
synonyms: Working well together turns differences into insight.
cards.notes: Read this as a reflection, not a factual rule. Relate it to a specific action in the example, and explain why you agree or disagree.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Good collaboration makes disagreement usable..

cards.title: Although / despite
cards.meaning: Use although before a clause, and despite before a noun phrase or an -ing form, to express contrast.
cards.example: Although time was limited, we tested the plan. Despite the time limit, we tested it.
cards.conversation:
A: Did the constraints stop the trial?
B: No. Despite having little time, we completed it.
A: Did the consultation change the plan?
B: Yes. We revised the entrance and simplified the labels.
cards.exercise: Rewrite with “despite”: Although the budget was limited, we consulted residents.
cards.answer: Despite the limited budget, we consulted residents.
cards.notes: Although the budget was limited; despite the limited budget; despite having little time. Do not write despite of.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Although / despite.

cards.title: Has this changed the way you approach teamwork?
cards.meaning: A reflective question about whether an experience has influenced someone's way of collaborating.
cards.example: Has this project changed the way you approach teamwork?
cards.conversation:
A: Has this changed the way you approach teamwork?
B: Yes. I now ask about expectations much earlier.
A: Which expectations would you ask about first?
B: Who can decide, who should be consulted, and what success means.
cards.exercise: Ask a thoughtful follow-up.
cards.answer: Which expectation would you clarify first next time?
cards.notes: The present perfect connects a past experience with the person's current approach. Invite an example rather than assuming change occurred.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Has this changed the way you approach teamwork?.

cards.title: Making disagreement productive
cards.meaning: Why constructive disagreement can strengthen collective judgement.
paragraphs: Collaboration gains value from constructive disagreement, not merely smooth agreement. Two conditions make dissent productive: a shared purpose that disciplines the discussion and relevant evidence that helps participants revise their views.

A shared purpose gives disagreement a useful boundary. In a community exhibition project, debates about the format initially reflected personal preferences. Once the team agreed that residents’ access mattered most, we could distinguish essential requirements from choices open to negotiation.

Evidence then turns that common purpose into better decisions. Residents’ feedback revealed that the proposed layout was difficult to navigate. This concrete finding allowed us to reconcile accessibility with creative ambitions, replacing competing tastes with a problem we could solve together.

Constructive disagreement thus depends on both common aims and a willingness to respond to evidence. Consensus is more valuable when it emerges from this inquiry. Good collaboration makes the reasoning behind agreement visible rather than treating agreement itself as proof of success.
cards.exercise: According to the essay, what makes disagreement productive?
cards.answer: A shared purpose, a distinction between requirements and preferences, and visible reasoning help turn disagreement into useful inquiry.
cards.example: We use “Making disagreement productive” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State two conditions for productive dissent. Develop shared purpose and evidence in separate example-led paragraphs. Synthesise their contribution to sound agreement.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Making disagreement productive.

cards.title: reciprocity
cards.meaning: The practice or principle of mutual exchange, response, or obligation.
cards.example: Meaningful reciprocity cannot always be reduced to an exchange of equal favours.
cards.conversation:
A: Must each contribution be identical?
B: No. Reciprocity can accommodate different capacities.
A: Does reciprocity require equal contributions?
B: Not identical ones, but some recognition of mutual obligation.
cards.exercise: Why is “reciprocity” broader than an immediate exchange?
cards.answer: It can involve mutual responsiveness over time rather than equal, immediate returns.
cards.synonymNote: Mutuality is broader; reciprocity often involves a responding act or obligation.
cards.notes: Usually uncountable. Reciprocity need not imply identical contributions, immediate repayment, or perfectly equal power.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating reciprocity.

cards.title: circumscribe
cards.meaning: To restrict something within defined boundaries.
cards.example: The brief circumscribes the committee’s authority without dictating every decision.
cards.conversation:
A: Can the committee change the project’s purpose?
B: No. Its authority is circumscribed by the brief.
A: Would those limits prevent useful action?
B: They could clarify which decisions require wider consent.
cards.exercise: Complete: The brief ____ the committee’s authority.
cards.answer: circumscribes
cards.synonymNote: Delimit stresses defining boundaries; restrict stresses limiting freedom or scope.
cards.notes: A formal verb, often used of authority, discretion, or possibilities. It emphasises setting limits rather than necessarily eliminating something.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating circumscribe.

cards.title: bear on
cards.meaning: To be relevant to, or have an effect on, a matter under consideration.
cards.example: The history of the site bears directly on the proposed design.
cards.conversation:
A: Is the earlier dispute relevant?
B: Yes. It bears on how residents interpret the proposal.
A: So procedural fairness is not the whole question?
B: Correct. We must also ask whose experiences the process recognises.
cards.exercise: Rewrite with “bear on”: This evidence is relevant to our decision.
cards.answer: This evidence bears on our decision.
cards.notes: Use bear on a question, judgement, or outcome. It does not mean physically carrying something in this sense.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating bear on.

cards.title: hold in tension
cards.meaning: To recognise competing ideas or values without prematurely resolving or dismissing either.
cards.example: We must hold openness and accountability in tension.
cards.conversation:
A: Can one principle settle the matter?
B: Probably not. We need to hold both concerns in tension.
A: Must we choose one value over the other?
B: Not immediately; preserving the tension can improve the decision.
cards.exercise: What does this phrase suggest about conflicting values?
cards.answer: They may need to coexist without being reduced to a single simple rule.
cards.notes: Common in analytical discussion. Holding two values in tension allows their competing demands to remain visible.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating hold in tension.

cards.title: move the goalposts
cards.meaning: To change the requirements for success after a process has begun.
cards.example: Changing the criteria after submission felt like moving the goalposts.
cards.conversation:
A: The proposal met every published requirement.
B: Then adding a new condition now would move the goalposts.
A: Could the new requirement still be justified?
B: Yes, but its rationale and consequences should be made explicit.
cards.exercise: Why might this expression imply unfairness?
cards.answer: People are judged against criteria that changed after they acted.
cards.notes: Usually critical: the speaker suggests the change is unfair or makes achievement unnecessarily difficult.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating move the goalposts.

cards.title: the devil is in the detail
cards.meaning: A saying that apparently minor details can determine whether a plan succeeds or creates difficulties.
cards.example: The agreement sounds fair, but the devil is in the detail.
cards.conversation:
A: Everyone supports shared ownership.
B: Yes, but the devil is in the detail: who can veto a decision?
A: Which detail could alter the outcome?
B: Who has the authority to revisit the decision.
cards.exercise: Give one detail that could complicate shared ownership.
cards.answer: The rules governing who can veto a decision.
synonyms: small points can cause big problems
cards.notes: Use it to direct attention to implementation. Detail is commonly singular in this established form, though details also occurs.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating the devil is in the detail.

cards.title: Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible.
cards.meaning: An agreement has substance only if people are still free to express disagreement.
cards.example: Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible.
cards.conversation:
A: Nobody objected during the meeting.
B: Did everyone feel able to object?
A: Would allowing objections guarantee a sound decision?
B: No. It is a necessary condition in this claim, not a sufficient one.
cards.exercise: Paraphrase the sentence without “dissent”.
cards.answer: Agreement matters only if people are free to express disagreement.
synonyms: Real consent requires room for disagreement.
A shared position must permit challenge.
cards.notes: Only when sets a necessary condition. It does not claim that allowing dissent is sufficient to make every agreement legitimate.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible..

cards.title: A collective voice should not erase the voices that compose it.
cards.meaning: A group's shared position should preserve accountability to the different people within it.
cards.example: A unanimous statement can conceal unresolved concerns. A collective voice should not erase the voices that compose it.
cards.conversation:
A: Should we remove the minority view from the report?
B: No. We can document it alongside the decision.
A: How could the group preserve those differences?
B: By recording unresolved concerns and explaining how they affected the decision.
cards.exercise: Explain the tension in this reflection.
cards.answer: A group needs a shared position while still acknowledging the distinct views of its members.
synonyms: A shared position should preserve individual perspectives.
cards.notes: Read this as a reflection, not a factual rule. Relate it to a specific action in the example, and explain why you agree or disagree.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating A collective voice should not erase the voices that compose it..

cards.title: Not until… did…
cards.meaning: After a fronted Not until phrase or clause, invert the auxiliary and subject in the main clause.
cards.example: Not until the assumptions were made explicit did the disagreement become manageable.
cards.conversation:
A: When did the discussion improve?
B: Not until we named the underlying assumptions did we make progress.
A: Why is did placed before the subject?
B: The fronted negative expression triggers inversion in the main clause.
cards.exercise: Rewrite: We understood the objection only after we read the full account.
cards.answer: Not until we had read the full account did we understand the objection.
cards.notes: Not until everyone had spoken did we vote. Keep normal word order inside the until-clause; inversion follows it.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating Not until… did….

cards.title: What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?
cards.meaning: A question inviting scrutiny of a belief that a discussion may have taken for granted.
cards.example: What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?
cards.conversation:
A: What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?
B: That everyone had the same freedom to participate.
A: How might we test that assumption?
B: We could ask whose evidence or experience might challenge it.
cards.exercise: Offer a follow-up that invites nuance rather than a yes/no answer.
cards.answer: How might unequal freedom to participate have shaped the apparent consensus?
cards.notes: Unexamined does not necessarily mean false. Ask what evidence or alternative perspective might test the assumption.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?.

cards.title: The limits of consensus
cards.meaning: An examination of the conditions under which consensus can support legitimate collective action.
paragraphs: Consensus can legitimise collective action, but unanimity alone proves little. Agreement deserves authority when participation is substantively fair and decisions remain open to revision; these conditions matter more than the appearance of complete alignment.

Fair participation requires scrutiny of how alternatives are framed. A neighbourhood committee may vote unanimously for a venue after consulting only residents who can attend evening meetings. The result appears orderly, yet excludes relevant experience. Such omissions bear on legitimacy even when formal procedures are followed.

Revisability provides a second safeguard against premature closure. The committee could circumscribe its decision-making authority, record objections and review the venue after a trial event. This approach enables action while preserving a route for overlooked needs to influence the outcome.

Legitimate consensus therefore combines inclusive deliberation with accountable revision. It holds decisiveness and openness in tension, allowing people to act together without pretending that differences have disappeared. A collective voice earns authority by remaining answerable to its constituent voices.
cards.exercise: Why does the writer distinguish unanimity from legitimate agreement?
cards.answer: Unanimity can result from deference or exclusion, so legitimacy depends on the conditions of participation and the continuing possibility of disagreement.
cards.example: We use “The limits of consensus” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Qualify the claim that consensus legitimises action. Examine inclusive participation, then revisability, using a connected example. Synthesize the conditions of legitimate agreement.

highlights.text: holds decisiveness and openness in tension

cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
cards.illustrationAlt: Original family-manga scene illustrating The limits of consensus.
